The Fever Breaks
nodes.description: Alexander recovers from his illness and secures his existing empire.

nodes.label: The Arabian Campaign
nodes.description: Alexander secures coastal routes and strengthens his position.

nodes.label: Building the Fleet
nodes.description: A fleet is assembled to challenge Carthage.

nodes.label: The War at Sea
nodes.description: The struggle for control of the western Mediterranean begins.

nodes.label: A Different Mediterranean
nodes.description: Greek influence expands westward while Rome follows a different political path.

nodes.label: The library survives
nodes.description: Caesar's fire damages the harbour district but leaves the library intact.

nodes.label: Alexandria's scientific centre
nodes.description: Scholars and engineers develop a continuous research tradition.

nodes.label: Early mechanization
nodes.description: Mechanical power finds wider use in mines, workshops, and agriculture.

nodes.label: Knowledge crosses cultures
nodes.description: Alexandria connects Greek scholarship with Arabic, Persian, and Indian intellectual traditions.

nodes.label: Scientific continuity
nodes.description: Knowledge accumulates through connected scholarly institutions rather than repeated rediscovery.

nodes.label: The Aztecs Reach Europe
nodes.description: An Aztec expedition crosses the Atlantic and reaches Portugal.

nodes.label: First Diplomatic Contacts
nodes.description: Aztec envoys establish relations with European rulers.

nodes.label: A New Atlantic Order Emerges
nodes.description: Contact between the two civilizations reshapes trade and political alliances.

nodes.label: The nuclear exchange
nodes.description: The Cuban Missile Crisis escalates into a nuclear exchange between the United States and the Soviet Union.

nodes.label: Nuclear winter
nodes.description: Nuclear fallout and climatic disruption devastate agriculture and cause widespread famine.

nodes.label: The surviving south
nodes.description: Countries in the Southern Hemisphere preserve more of their population and institutional capacity.

nodes.label: A different world order
nodes.description: Surviving powers in the Global South shape a radically different international order.

nodes.label: The Umayyads win at Tours
nodes.description: The Frankish defeat creates an opportunity for further Muslim expansion into Western Europe.

nodes.label: Muslim rule expands into France
nodes.description: If political stability and military success continue, parts of Western Europe come under lasting Islamic rule.

nodes.label: Intellectual and cultural exchange grows
nodes.description: Arabic scholarship, European traditions, and knowledge from across the Islamic world interact in new centres of learning.

nodes.label: A different age of exploration
nodes.description: Political and maritime developments may lead to different patterns of Atlantic exploration and overseas expansion.

nodes.label: A different conception of Europe
nodes.description: Religious, linguistic, and political identities develop along a path unlike the historical division between Europe and the Islamic world.

nodes.label: The French fleet survives Aboukir Bay
nodes.description: Nelson's attack fails, and French naval presence in the Eastern Mediterranean is preserved.

nodes.label: French control over Egypt is consolidated
nodes.description: Napoleon remains in the East and builds a permanent administration.

nodes.label: The Levant campaign succeeds
nodes.description: French forces take Acre and push into Syria.

nodes.label: An Eastern French empire emerges
nodes.description: Egypt and the Levant become a permanent part of the French sphere.

nodes.label: The empire survives
nodes.description: The Western Roman state avoids final collapse.

nodes.label: A smaller Rome
nodes.description: The empire consolidates a more limited territory in the western Mediterranean.

nodes.label: Roman continuity
nodes.description: Roman law, Latin, and imperial institutions persist in altered forms.

nodes.label: A different Europe
nodes.description: Europe develops without the familiar historical divide between Rome and the Middle Ages.

nodes.label: The landing succeeds
nodes.description: The Armada escorts Parma's army across the Channel.

nodes.label: Catholic restoration
nodes.description: England's religious settlement is overturned amid conflict and resistance.

nodes.label: A different balance of power
nodes.description: Spain's influence expands, but the cost of controlling England strains its empire.

nodes.label: No British Empire as we know it
nodes.description: Global trade and colonial expansion develop along a different path.

nodes.label: The fall of Vienna
nodes.description: Ottoman forces capture the Habsburg capital.

nodes.label: The Ottoman advance
nodes.description: The fall of Vienna changes the strategic balance in Central Europe.

nodes.label: France fills the vacuum
nodes.description: France expands its influence as European powers adjust to the altered balance.

nodes.label: A different Enlightenment
nodes.description: Intellectual and political developments unfold under a different continental order.

nodes.label: Napoleon wins Waterloo
nodes.description: Without the decisive Prussian intervention, the French break Wellington's army.

nodes.label: France consolidates its position
nodes.description: The coalition loses the political leverage needed to impose the historical settlement.

nodes.label: A new European order emerges
nodes.description: France becomes the dominant continental power, while Britain remains its principal rival.

nodes.label: The succession question
nodes.description: Napoleon's age turns succession and imperial continuity into central political questions.

nodes.label: The Napoleonic system begins to decline
nodes.description: The empire survives, but its institutions become increasingly difficult to sustain.

nodes.label: The asteroid misses Earth
nodes.description: The impact never occurs and the Cretaceous extinction event unfolds differently.

nodes.label: Dinosaurs continue to diversify
nodes.description: Non-avian dinosaurs remain dominant across Earth's terrestrial ecosystems.

nodes.label: Mammals remain in the shadows
nodes.description: Without the extinction of the dinosaurs, mammals do not receive the same evolutionary opportunity to diversify.

nodes.label: A different path to intelligence
nodes.description: Some dinosaur lineages may evolve increasingly complex behaviour and intelligence, though the outcome remains uncertain.

nodes.label: A very different Earth
nodes.description: Earth remains dominated by ecosystems shaped by dinosaurs rather than mammals and primates.

nodes.label: Mars retains its oceans and atmosphere
nodes.description: Mars remains warm and wet instead of losing its surface water and thick atmosphere.

nodes.label: Humanity observes a blue Mars
nodes.description: Mars appears as a visibly active and potentially habitable world in the night sky.

nodes.label: The race for Mars
nodes.description: The space age becomes a race to reach and study a living neighbouring world.

nodes.label: Permanent research bases become possible
nodes.description: Long-term human research presence on Mars becomes conceivable.

nodes.label: Human settlements beyond Earth
nodes.description: Humanity may establish its first permanent settlements beyond Earth.

nodes.label: The Web is never proposed
nodes.description: The system designed to make information sharing between computers simple and universal never emerges.

nodes.label: Information networks remain fragmented
nodes.description: Commercial online services, telephone networks, television, and private computer systems develop independently.

nodes.label: Global collaboration slows
nodes.description: Scientific research, open-source software, online education, and international communication lack the Web's universal platform.

nodes.label: Alternative digital ecosystems expand
nodes.description: Regional and commercial networks grow, potentially divided by national borders, corporate control, and political blocs.

nodes.label: A world of information islands
nodes.description: People still communicate through technology, but access to knowledge and global participation remain more fragmented.
